There is an allusion here to debates in Russian philosophy and politics concerning sexuality and the family, with Kojève here taking the “Stalinist” side. See L. Trotsky, The Revolution Betrayed, op. cit., especially Chapter VII, “The Family, Youth, and Culture,” section “Thermidor in the Family”:

“The revolution made a heroic effort to destroy the so-called ‘family hearth’—that archaic, stuffy and stagnant institution in which the woman of the toiling classes performs galley labor from childhood to death. The place of the family as a shut-in petty enterprise was to be occupied, according to the plans, by a finished system of social care and accommodation: maternity houses, crèches, kindergartens […] etc. The complete absorption of the housekeeping functions of the family by institutions of the socialist society, uniting all generations in solidarity and mutual aid, was to bring to woman, and thereby to the loving couple, a real liberation from the thousand-year-old fetters. Until this task is fulfilled forty million Soviet families, in their overwhelming majority, will remain nests of medievalism, female slavery and hysteria.”

“The solemn rehabilitation of the family [by the Stalinist faction, of which Kojève is here a representative] […] is the result of the material and cultural bankruptcy of the state. Instead of openly saying: ‘We have proved still too poor and ignorant for the creation of socialist relations among men, our children and great-grandchildren will realize this aim,’ the leaders are forcing people to glue together again the shell of the broken family, and not only that, but to consider it, under threat of extreme penalties, the sacred nucleus of triumphant socialism. It is difficult to measure with the eye the scope of this retreat!”

From a strictly historical point of view, this is a rather questionable claim. Stalin is generally thought to have had little sympathy for Hegel and even to have tried, as far as possible, to suppress the Hegelian inheritance within the thought of Marx and Lenin. In his study Hegel in Russia, Guy Planty-Bonjour recalls this political campaign, which went so far as effectively to censor Lenin himself:

If one is convinced that Marx owes practically nothing to the German philosopher, one naturally tends to minimize the importance of the Philosophical Notebooks [Lenin’s notes from 1914–15 on the Science of Logic, the Lectures on the History of Philosophy, and the Lectures on the Philosophy of History], or even to deny their value altogether: Lenin’s thought would then be contained entirely in Materialism and Empirio-Criticism. This was the dominant interpretation in the Soviet Union during the Stalinist period. As M. Garaudy observes, the Philosophical Notebooks “were excluded under Stalin from Lenin’s Collected Works, just as the 1844 Manuscripts were excluded from Marx’s Works, because they were incompatible with a dogmatic interpretation of Marxism.”

Lenin had indeed written his notes on the Science of Logic. But Stalin effectively prevented their circulation. Lenin therefore influenced the development of Soviet philosophy through the anti-Hegelian book Materialism and Empirio-Criticism.
See G. Planty-Bonjour, Hegel et la pensée philosophique en Russie, 1830–1917, The Hague: Martinus Nijhoff, 1974, pp. 281 and 332. (Translator’s note.)↩

This is a quotation from Lenin’s 1908 article “Leo Tolstoy as the Mirror of the Russian Revolution.” Tolstoy (1828–1910) is presented there as a mirror of the 1905 Revolution. As Lenin emphasizes, however, if Tolstoy is a mirror of the revolution, this also means that the revolution was not a clear or homogeneous movement. Religious philosophy itself, especially in the form of Tolstoyanism, took part in it in its own way, without understanding what it was doing—that is, unconsciously. (Translator’s note.)↩

In Russian, Kojève uses javlenie (“appearance” or “appearing”) and fenomen (“phenomenon”). We have tried to preserve this distinction as far as possible because Kojève himself writes in the margin of the manuscript: “‘Appearing’ = ‘phenomenon’ + how + to whom.” We have therefore translated javlenie sometimes as “appearance” and sometimes as “appearing.” In a note to this book dated 15 February 1941 (folio 939), Kojève supports the translation of javlenie as “appearing,” although in French it has occasionally seemed necessary to translate it as “apparition” in order to preserve natural usage.↩
Kojève underlined these words—the Russian poznanie—and placed a question mark in the margin. It should also be noted that Erfahrung is normally translated as “experience.” (Translator’s note.)↩

For the sake of clarity, the French editors chose at this point to translate poznanie as “experience” or “cognitive experience,” following the usual French translation of Hegel’s Erfahrung. Kojève eventually placed Erfahrung alongside poznanie himself, though with a question mark.

Earlier in the text, poznanie had generally been rendered as “cognition,” which is closer to its primary meaning, though “experience” was sometimes used for samo-poznanie in order to distinguish it from “self-knowledge” (znanie sebja).

In general, however, cognition can be understood as an experience through which knowledge advances. This also brings us close to the original sense of the German Erfahrung, which is related to fahren, “to travel” or “to go”: experience understood as a kind of movement or progression.

In any case, when Kojève speaks of a “cognition of oneself,” the editors judged “experience” to be the more natural term. In French, as in English, we would normally speak of the experience one has of oneself rather than one’s “cognition of oneself.”
That is what is at issue here: knowing oneself by experiencing oneself—even if, in the end, that experience expands to the dimensions of the entire world.↩

It is very difficult to reproduce in French Kojève’s use of the Russian word nečto, which the French editors render, for lack of anything better, as “something.” This should not be taken to mean that the human being is a “thing” in the Russian sense of vešč’. Kojève’s point is precisely that the human being is not a “thing” but “something” other than a thing. He also plays on the Russian words when he writes that this nečto samo po sebe — ničto: this “something, in itself, is nothing.” The wordplay cannot be reproduced exactly in French. (Translator’s note.)↩

The distinction is subtle in French but important. Kojève distinguishes nečto drugoe, “something different” or “another thing,” from nečto inoe, “something other.” The distinction becomes clearer in light of one of his earliest important texts, Atheism (1931). There Kojève tries to understand the status of God as the radically Other—something transcending both world and human beings. God, in this sense, is not merely “something different,” nečto drugoe: one other thing among others, and therefore something that could still be encountered within the world. God is instead the radically “other,” inoe: the Other par excellence, the other of all other things, something that cannot be reduced to an object within the world. Kojève later associates this radical Other with “nothingness,” the “other” of being. The French editors therefore render nečto inoe as “quelque chose autre,” “something other,” rather than allowing it to collapse into the ordinary “something different.” (Translator’s note.)↩

Kojève writes čelovečnost’, which can mean “humanity” in the sense of the quality or character of being human. Russian has another word, čelovečestvo, for “humanity” in the sense of humankind as a whole, and Kojève deliberately plays on the distinction. Later in the book, for example, he can speak of “the degree of humanity (čelovečnost’) attained by humanity (čelovečestvo).” In English, the first sense could also be rendered as “humanness” to make the distinction explicit.↩

Publisher’s Preface to the Second Edition
Publisher’s Preface to the Second Edition
Publisher’s Preface to the Second Edition

This book first appeared in the 1970s. We printed ten thousand copies, and every one of them sold. We have long felt that it deserved to be published again, both because of the importance of its subject and because of the importance of its author. When I asked Khaled Mohieddin for permission to reissue it, he readily agreed.
Publisher’s Preface to the Second Edition

Mohieddin is a leading figure of the Egyptian left, and the question he raises in this book is both important and urgent. He believes in socialism and argues for it within a society whose dominant faith is Islam. With evidence and argument, he answers those who insist on setting socialism against Islam, and shows that both socialism and Islam call for social justice and democracy.
Publisher’s Preface to the Second Edition

Mohieddin was one of the founders of the Free Officers movement, which planned and carried out the July Revolution with overwhelming popular support. Both before and after the revolution, he argued that democracy had to go hand in hand with social justice. The Revolutionary Command Council brought together people with different political outlooks, united by their determination to bring the old order to an end.
Publisher’s Preface to the Second Edition

The revolution succeeded, and Mohieddin was one of its leaders. But his commitment to democracy brought him into conflict with his colleagues when he believed democratic principles were being violated. This led him to spend two years abroad. After his return, Gamal Abdel Nasser put him in charge first of Al-Masaa and later Akhbar al-Yom. Mohieddin remained alongside Nasser throughout the major struggles of the national movement: the nationalization of the Suez Canal, resistance to the tripartite invasion, the later nationalizations, and the other national and social measures of the period. He supported these policies strongly because they reflected both his socialist convictions and his deep commitment to Egypt.
We do not claim that Islam is a socialist religion, nor do we claim that the Islamic idea of social justice is identical to socialism.

If we made that claim, our opponents would be equally entitled to argue that Islam is a capitalist religion, perfectly compatible with economic individualism, feudal privilege, class inequality, and social injustice.

The result would be predictable. Each side would search the Qur’an and the teachings of the Prophet for a verse or saying that appeared to support its own position, then twist those texts through interpretation until they seemed to endorse whatever political ideas it wanted to spread.

We have seen this before in Muslim history, and it led to consequences we have no wish to repeat. Muslims divided over political, social, and tribal questions, and some then made the mistake of giving those disagreements a religious character. Political and social conflict between people who shared the same faith was turned into religious conflict, with accusations of unbelief used as a weapon against opponents.
Ali ibn Abi Talib warned of exactly this danger when he said that the Qur’an can bear more than one interpretation, and when he described certain slogans as true words being used for a false purpose.
There is another problem as well.

Suppose we permanently tie religion to one particular social doctrine or economic system. History keeps moving. Society changes. Eventually that system may cease to be the best answer to the needs of ordinary people.
Would we not have tied religion to something whose historical moment had passed? Would we not have condemned religion to share the fate of ideas and movements that life itself had left behind?
That would contradict our belief that the basic principles of religion remain valid in every age and place.

We reject this entire way of thinking. We also call on everyone engaged in political and social life in our country to stop trying to force religion into the box of one particular economic system or social doctrine.
But one question remains: what is the relationship between Islam, as a religion, and the social doctrines competing in our society today?

Those doctrines reflect the different and often conflicting interests of different social classes. So where does Islam stand in relation to them? Which social interests does it support? Which groups does it favour in this struggle?

We believe there is a real relationship between the basic principles of Islamic thought and the solutions that different social systems offer to human problems. Islam is not a religion cut off from the affairs and problems of earthly life.
But we do not believe that this relationship takes the form of ready-made solutions and complete social systems waiting in old books for modern people to discover and put into practice.

What Islam gives us instead is something more fundamental: its enduring call for social justice; fairness between human beings; a view of the community as one interconnected whole; and the principle that the interests of society as a whole, and of its majority, should take priority over the interests of a smaller group when the two come into conflict.
The social justice called for by Islam is best understood as an ideal.

Human beings continually move toward it, hoping to make it real in everyday life. Each time society comes closer to that ideal and achieves a greater degree of justice, we discover that the road still stretches ahead of us—and that it is a long one. Greater justice creates the need for still greater justice.
Human needs and aspirations have no final limit. Neither does humanity’s hope for a more just life on this earth.
Once we understand both this central Islamic commitment to social justice and the fact that economic and social systems continually develop and change, the issue becomes much clearer.

Social movements and doctrines that seek greater justice for the broad mass of people are moving along the road toward which Islam points and which the Prophet proclaimed. Economic conditions change, and social doctrines change with them. Their names and forms change too.

But one principle remains: those who seek, through their social system, to bring the greatest possible degree of social justice to the broadest possible majority are moving ever closer to the ideal of justice proclaimed by Islam.
In the language of Muslim jurists:
Wherever the welfare of the community lies, there lies God’s law.
These are the basic principles that shape Islam’s position on social justice in this life. We find them in the Qur’an and in the teachings of the Prophet:
The earth and all the wealth it contains were created for humanity as a whole, not for a small, privileged minority that exploits and dominates everyone else:
